uncited: This family defines the mathematical and algorithmic framework for applying rigid body transformations—rotations and translations—to 3D geometry and camera poses within volume rendering pipelines.
It solves the problem of mapping coordinates between different reference frames (e.g., local cell space to world space, or camera space to world space) while preserving distances and angles.

It is distinguished from [Rotation Transformation](2279-rotation-transformation.md) and [Translation Transformation](2281-translation-transformation.md) by treating rotation and translation as a single coupled operation in the Special Euclidean group $SE(3)$, and from [Pose Recentering](1786-pose-recentering.md) by its general applicability to any rigid mapping rather than just centering.
The family operates on the Special Euclidean group $SE(3)$, which consists of all rigid transformations in 3D space.
A rigid transformation $T$ is defined by a rotation matrix $R \in SO(3)$ and a translation vector $t \in \mathbb{R}^3$.
To perform these operations linearly, points and vectors are represented in homogeneous coordinates.
A 3D point $p = (x, y, z)$ is represented as $p_h = (x, y, z, 1)^T$, while a direction vector $v = (x, y, z)$ is represented as $v_h = (x, y, z, 0)^T$.
The distinction is critical: appending 1 allows translation to affect the position, while appending 0 ensures translation does not affect the direction.
where $R$ is a $3 \times 3$ orthogonal matrix with determinant 1, and $t$ is a $3 \times 1$ column vector.
The bottom row is $[0, 0, 0, 1]$ to preserve the homogeneous coordinate.
The mathematical foundation of rigid body transformations in 3D space is rooted in the Special Euclidean group $SE(3)$.
In the context of volume rendering and computer graphics, this group is essential for defining camera poses and transforming geometric primitives between local and world coordinate systems.
The specific implementation details of `RigidXform` originate from the Spall project, a CPU-only volume rendering engine.
The optimization technique using sine/cosine decomposition for $SE(3)$ poses was developed for training generative radiance fields, specifically within the `mrGSplat` project.
